## Replications of published analyses

This is one of the replication vignettes (16 to 20 and 22 to 24). The inputs are tables
printed in the paper's supporting information, every result is shown beside the
published one, and the same comparisons are in the test suite
(`test/fixtures/replications/christensen2026_turtle.json`, `test/test_replications.jl`).

## The paper

Christensen, McGowan and Lawson (2026), "Using value of information in recovery planning
for imperiled species", *Conservation Science and Practice* e70421,
[doi:10.1111/csp2.70421](https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70421), CC BY 4.0. The inputs are
Tables S4, S5 and S7 of the supporting information and the targets Table 3 of the
article.

**Decision.** Which recovery strategy to adopt for the western analysis unit of the
alligator snapping turtle (*Macrochelys temminckii*).

**Actions.** Five strategies: reduce the spatial extent of recreational bycatch and hook
ingestion by 30%, of illegal collection, or of subsidised nest predation; reduce the
magnitude of bycatch and hook ingestion by 30%; or head-start hatchlings. No action is
the `baseline`.

**States.** Experts' estimates of the magnitude (M) and the extent (E) of the threats may
each be overestimated (1), accurate (2) or underestimated (3): nine hypotheses, weighted
by a bivariate normal density (0.28 for the centre, 0.125 for an edge, 0.055 for a
corner).

**Outcome.** Three measures from the authors' population model, each the mean of 1,000
simulations: the population growth rate, the years added to the expected time to
extirpation, and adult fecundity. The paper turns each into a decision-maker's value
between 0 and 1 with four hypothetical value functions. **No cost appears in the
paper.** The population model is not rerun here; this vignette recomputes the
value-of-information layer on its printed outputs.

```{julia}
using DecisionAnalysis
include(joinpath("..", "_common.jl"))

actions = [:reduce_extent_bycatch, :reduce_extent_collection, :reduce_extent_nest_predators,
           :reduce_magnitude_bycatch, :head_start, :no_action]
states = [:M1E1, :M1E2, :M1E3, :M2E1, :M2E2, :M2E3, :M3E1, :M3E2, :M3E3]
weights = [55, 125, 55, 125, 280, 125, 55, 125, 55] .// 1000
# Rows = hypotheses, columns = actions. Table S4 (linear block): population growth rate.
lambda = [0.9564 0.9552 0.9523 0.9532 0.9525 0.9524; 0.9335 0.9313 0.9242 0.9255 0.9241 0.9244;
          0.9069 0.9040 0.8928 0.8946 0.8929 0.8930; 0.9265 0.9247 0.9195 0.9266 0.9192 0.9193;
          0.8851 0.8808 0.8676 0.8796 0.8673 0.8671; 0.8357 0.8304 0.8100 0.8283 0.8104 0.8099;
          0.8834 0.8792 0.8717 0.8892 0.8714 0.8715; 0.8144 0.8062 0.7852 0.8152 0.7855 0.7852;
          0.7341 0.7229 0.6921 0.7340 0.6910 0.6920]
# Table S5: years added to the expected time to extirpation.
years = [4 2 1 3 1 0; 15 11 0 2 0 0; 12 9 0 1 0 0; 10 7 0 10 0 0; 10 8 0 7 0 0;
         8 6 0 5 1 0; 7 5 0 11 1 0; 7 4 0 7 0 0; 5 3 0 5 2 0]
# Table S7 (linear block): adult fecundity.
fecundity = [0.2909 0.2697 0.2778 0.2773 0.2906 0.2773; 0.2624 0.2612 0.2836 0.2707 0.2679 0.2762;
             0.2600 0.2411 0.2687 0.2557 0.2650 0.2691; 0.2754 0.2746 0.2846 0.2693 0.2670 0.2710;
             0.2436 0.2347 0.2643 0.2398 0.2337 0.2263; 0.1982 0.2284 0.2449 0.2161 0.2189 0.2090;
             0.2365 0.2460 0.2643 0.2458 0.2527 0.2414; 0.1952 0.2085 0.2451 0.1996 0.2061 0.2069;
             0.1821 0.1735 0.2083 0.1684 0.1627 0.1747]
problem(values) = DecisionProblem(PayoffTable(actions, states, permutedims(values)),
                                  FiniteBelief(states, weights); baseline=:no_action)
problem(years).payoff
```

## In years, before any value function

```{julia}
by_years = problem(years)
md_table(["action", "expected years added (paper, Table S5)", "this package", "chosen"],
         [[a, p, Float64(e), a in decide(by_years, MaxExpectedUtility()).chosen]
          for (a, p, e) in zip(actions, (9.34, 6.785, 0.055, 6.06, 0.345, 0),
                               expected_gain_over_baseline(by_years))]; digits=3)
```

Years are counted from no action, so each entry is already a gain over the baseline.
Reducing the extent of bycatch adds most, 9.34 years on average, and learning the true
hypothesis first would add `{julia} round(Float64(evpi(by_years)); digits=2)` years
more: reducing the *magnitude* of bycatch is better only when the threat magnitude was
underestimated and its extent overestimated.

## The value functions

The paper applies four curves: `V = x`, and three logistic curves
`V = scale / (1 + exp(-12 (x - midpoint))) + shift`. Growth rate and fecundity enter
unscaled, and years are divided by 25.

```{julia}
logistic(scale, midpoint, shift) = x -> scale / (1 + exp(-12 * (x - midpoint))) + shift
curves = ["convex" => logistic(1.5, 0.05, -0.5), "linear" => identity,
          "S-curve" => logistic(1.0, 0.5, 0.0), "concave" => logistic(1.3, 0.9, 0.0)]
metrics = ["growth rate" => lambda, "time to extirpation" => years ./ 25,
           "fecundity" => fecundity]
table3 = [(0.9999, 0.9999, 0.0000), (0.8780, 0.8785, 0.0005), (0.9865, 0.9866, 0.0001),
          (0.5768, 0.5784, 0.0016), (0.9381, 0.9422, 0.0041), (0.3736, 0.3824, 0.0088),
          (0.2413, 0.2557, 0.0144), (0.0064, 0.0066, 0.0002), (0.8887, 0.8894, 0.0007),
          (0.2623, 0.2631, 0.0008), (0.0557, 0.0563, 0.0006), (0.0006, 0.0006, 0.0000)]
rows, k = Vector{Any}[], 0
for (metric, values) in metrics, (curve, f) in curves
    global k += 1
    p = problem(f.(values))
    push!(rows,
          [metric, curve, first(decide(p, MaxExpectedUtility()).chosen), table3[k][1],
           act_now_value(p), table3[k][2], act_now_value(p) + evpi(p), table3[k][3], evpi(p)])
end
md_table(["measure", "curve", "chosen", "paper: uncertainty", "ours", "paper: certainty",
          "ours", "paper: EVPI", "ours"], rows; digits=4)
```

All twelve rows of Table 3 are reproduced, and the same action is chosen as in the paper:
reducing the extent of bycatch for the growth rate and for the time to extirpation, and
reducing the extent of nest predation for fecundity. (Under the convex curve every
action has the same value of the growth rate to four decimals.)

Three things differ from the print, and the reasons are known.

- **The paper's EVPI is the difference of the two rounded values.** For the largest
  case, time to extirpation under the S-curve, it prints 0.0144 and 5.97%; unrounded
  they are 0.0143 and 5.94%.
- **The concave curve as printed does not give the paper's own tables.** The supporting
  information prints `2 / (1 + exp(-12 (x - 1)))`. The concave columns of its Tables S4,
  S6 and S7 are instead matched, in every cell, by `1.3 / (1 + exp(-12 (x - 0.9)))`,
  which is **our fit** and is printed nowhere. The table above uses the fitted curve;
  the printed one gives the following.
- **No action under the time to extirpation** is printed as zero under every curve,
  though the convex and S-curves give 0.0315 and 0.0025 at zero years. No action is never
  best, so no value depends on it; the table above applies the curves throughout.

```{julia}
as_printed = problem(logistic(2.0, 1.0, 0.0).(lambda))
md_table(["growth rate, concave curve", "value under uncertainty"],
         [["paper, Table 3", 0.5768], ["the curve as printed", act_now_value(as_printed)],
          ["the fitted curve", act_now_value(problem(logistic(1.3, 0.9, 0.0).(lambda)))]];
         digits=4)
```

## Magnitude or extent (ours)

The paper values the nine hypotheses together. The same tables give the value of
learning only the magnitude, or only the extent; these numbers are **ours, not the
paper's**.

```{julia}
magnitude, extent = [div(s - 1, 3) for s in 1:9], [mod1(s, 3) for s in 1:9]
rows = Vector{Any}[]
for (metric, values) in metrics[2:2], (curve, f) in curves
    p = problem(f.(values))
    push!(rows, [metric, curve, evppi(p, magnitude), evppi(p, extent), evpi(p)])
end
md_table(["measure", "curve", "magnitude alone", "extent alone", "both (EVPI)"], rows; digits=4)
```

## What the replication shows

The value of information is small throughout because one action is best under nearly
every hypothesis, which is the paper's conclusion. It also depends on the value function
as much as on the biology: for the time to extirpation the same model outputs give an
EVPI of 0.4% of the expected value under the convex curve and 6% under the S-curve.
